Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old woman with known SLE on methotrexate presenting with acute onset (today) shortness of breath, right-sided pleuritic back pain on deep inspiration, cough with two brief episodes of hemoptysis, subjective feverishness and palpitations; remote assessment online felt hemodynamically stable but requires same-day in-person evaluation to exclude pneumonia, PE, or SLE-related pulmonary involvement.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Acute breathlessness and pleuritic right-sided back pain associated with cough and two episodes of blood-streaked sputum today.
  - Subjective feeling of being feverish (felt warm to touch).
  - Awareness of heart beating/palpitations.
  - Two weeks of increasing tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance preceding acute respiratory symptoms.
- Timeline:
  - ~2 weeks: progressive fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance.
  - Today (acute): onset of cough, pleuritic right-sided back pain on deep inspiration, two episodes of hemoptysis, subjective feverish sensation, awareness of heartbeat.
  - Symptoms worsened acutely today prompting contact.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Pain worse with deep inspiration and coughing.
  - No relieving factors described.
- Associated symptoms / systems review (as reported):
  - Cough with blood on two occasions.
  - Subjective fever (no measured temperature).
  - Palpitations/awareness of heartbeat.
  - No reported leg swelling, chest trauma, recent long-haul travel, or prior history of DVT/PE.
  - No other systemic SLE flare features documented (no rash, hematuria, or joint flare described).
- Pertinent negatives:
  - Patient denies smoking.
  - No drug allergies reported.
  - Patient reports no known prior clots and no family history of clots.
  - No measured vitals (temperature, BP, SpO2, RR) documented in transcript.

Past Medical History:
- Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
  - No details provided on disease manifestations, disease activity, or antiphospholipid antibody status.
- Medications:
  - Methotrexate — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports last dose taken this morning.
- Allergies:
  - None reported.

Social History:
- Lives alone in a flat.
- Occupation: office-based desk job.
- Smoking: denies tobacco use.
- Alcohol/substance use: not mentioned.
- Pets: cat.
- No recent long-haul travel reported.
- No other social/financial factors mentioned.

Family History:
- No family history of venous thromboembolism reported.
- Other family history details not provided.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals:
  - Radial pulse counted by patient (self-measure) ≈ 66–74 bpm (patient counted ~11–12 in 10 seconds; clinician interpreted as ~66–74 bpm).
  - No measured blood pressure, temperature, respiratory rate, or SpO2 reported.
- Examination findings from remote assessment:
  - Peripheral capillary refill appeared normal on video per clinician assessment.
  - Visual inspection of throat: unremarkable on video; patient said “ah” and clinician noted throat was visualized.
  - Cervical lymph nodes: patient palpated sides of neck and reported no enlarged glands.
- No chest auscultation performed (video/remote limitations).
- No abdominal, cardiovascular, or extremity exam findings documented.

Investigations:
- None performed during this consult.
- Remote/online assessments performed: patient self-counted radial pulse; clinician observed capillary refill and visualized oropharynx.
- No imaging, blood tests, ECG, or pulse oximetry recorded.

Assessment & Plan:
- Integrate transcript impressions with DDx: The clinician and the DDx both consider community-acquired pneumonia most likely, with pulmonary embolism and SLE-related pulmonary involvement also plausible given acute pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, SLE history and methotrexate immunosuppression. Patient appears not acutely unstable on remote assessment but requires in-person evaluation.

- Issue 1: Acute respiratory illness with hemoptysis — most likely community-acquired pneumonia (per clinician and DDx).
  - Assessment:
    - Acute onset cough, subjective fever, pleuritic right-sided pain and hemoptysis consistent with possible pneumonia/chest infection.
  - Plan (supported by transcript and DDx):
    - Arrange same-day face-to-face assessment with a GP/clinician for full physical exam including:
      - Chest auscultation.
      - Measured vital signs: temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and pulse oximetry (SpO2).
    - If clinical assessment supports infection, consider empiric oral antibiotics as indicated after face-to-face evaluation (clinician indicated possible need for antibiotics; no antibiotic prescribed remotely).
    - Consider chest X-ray during or after face-to-face review if clinical concern persists or symptoms do not rapidly improve (clinician noted possible follow-up chest X-ray if not settling).
    - Return precautions: escalate urgently if worsening shortness of breath, syncope, frank large-volume hemoptysis, new hypoxia, high fever or hemodynamic instability.

- Issue 2: Pulmonary embolism (PE) with possible pulmonary infarct — medium concern given acute pleuritic pain, hemoptysis and palpitations; SLE may increase thrombotic risk (DDx).
  - Assessment:
    - PE remains a differential given acute pleuritic pain and hemoptysis, though no classic provoking factors (recent travel, immobility) and remote pulse normal.
  - Plan (supported by transcript and DDx):
    - Urgent face-to-face assessment to measure SpO2, heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate and to assess clinical probability for PE.
    - If clinical suspicion for PE is raised on face-to-face review, investigate according to local pathways (e.g., D-dimer if low–moderate pretest probability; CT pulmonary angiography if indicated). (DDx recommends considering PE workup; clinician specifically queried risk factors and recommended in-person assessment.)
    - If patient unstable or hypoxic, arrange immediate emergency department transfer.

- Issue 3: SLE-related pulmonary involvement or methotrexate-related pulmonary disease — medium/low consideration.
  - Assessment:
    - SLE can cause lupus pneumonitis or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) which may present with hemoptysis and fever; methotrexate can cause pneumonitis or predispose to opportunistic infection.
  - Plan (supported by transcript and DDx):
    - In-person assessment and baseline investigations if indicated: consider chest X-ray and targeted blood tests (e.g., full blood count to check for anemia/hemoglobin drop, inflammatory markers) as clinically appropriate.
    - If DAH or severe autoimmune pulmonary process suspected on assessment (e.g., progressive respiratory compromise, falling hemoglobin, diffuse infiltrates on imaging), arrange urgent admission and rheumatology/respiratory input.
    - Continue to document methotrexate use in records; no instruction given in the consult to stop methotrexate remotely — defer management of immunosuppression to in-person team and specialists as clinically indicated.

- General plan items (supported by transcript/DDx):
  - Clinician arranged for support team to book a same-day face-to-face GP appointment and advised clinic assessment today.
  - No antibiotics or other medications were prescribed remotely; management contingent on face-to-face assessment.
  - Provide safety-netting advice: seek urgent care/ED if worsening dyspnea, large-volume hemoptysis, syncope, chest pain, or signs of sepsis.
  - Consider baseline investigations in clinic/ED as clinically indicated: chest X-ray (recommended by clinician/DDx), pulse oximetry and full vitals, and targeted blood tests; consider PE workup if clinically indicated.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- 1) Community-acquired pneumonia (bacterial pneumonia)
  - Likelihood: High
  - Rationale: Acute onset of cough with hemoptysis, subjective fever, and localized pleuritic pain; treating clinician also prioritized chest infection and recommended face-to-face chest auscultation and possible antibiotics.
- 2) Pulmonary embolism (with possible pulmonary infarct)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: Acute pleuritic pain, hemoptysis and palpitations are consistent with PE; SLE raises baseline thrombotic risk (possible antiphospholipid antibodies). No classic provoking history or abnormal vitals documented remotely, so PE remains possible but not definitively supported.
- 3) SLE-related pulmonary involvement (lupus pneumonitis or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: Known SLE predisposes to pulmonary vasculitis/DAH which can present acutely with hemoptysis and fever; lack of other systemic flare features and relative remote stability make this less certain but important to exclude.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs (measured temperature, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation) are not recorded.
  - No quantitative description of hemoptysis volume or character beyond “coughed up a bit of blood on two occasions.”
  - No laboratory results (FBC, CRP, D-dimer, renal/liver function, coagulation) or imaging (chest X-ray, CTPA) available.
  - Methotrexate dose, route and frequency not documented.
  - Antiphospholipid antibody status and recent SLE disease activity not provided.
  - Pregnancy status not documented (relevant when on methotrexate) — not asked/documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant — transcript and DDx are consistent (both prioritize chest infection, list PE and SLE-related pulmonary disease as important differentials). Conflict noted: none.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Audio/visual remote consultation transcript is generally clear; clinician performed limited visual assessments and guided patient self-examination. No major inaudible sections; some minor repetition and name confusion but overall adequate for documentation.
